Victor Hugo. Born in eighteen oh-two and dying in eighteen eighty-five, the towering figure of French Romanticism and one of Europe's greatest novelists, whose works defined French literature for generations. Through novels like Les Misérables and Notre-Dame de Paris, he championed the poor and outcast while crafting epic narratives of human suffering and redemption. His political activism and moral vision made him a national conscience—celebrated, exiled, and eventually canonized as France's literary giant.

Born into nobility, Hugo became an advocate for the poor and oppressed, a journey that shaped all his work. He first published poetry as a young man and was celebrated by King Louis the Eighteenth before his political views shifted decidedly left. Notre-Dame de Paris, published in eighteen thirty-one and also titled The Hunchback of Notre-Dame, was a sensation across Europe, blending Gothic atmosphere with social criticism. Les Misérables, published in eighteen sixty-two, is his masterwork—an epic novel of Jean Valjean's redemption, poverty, justice, and revolution set against Napoleonic France.

Hugo was exiled from France for nineteen years, from eighteen fifty-one to eighteen seventy, due to his opposition to Napoleon the Third. He spent those years in Belgium and the Channel Islands, continuing to write with undiminished power. He was also a significant poet and dramatist. His plays broke classical conventions and helped define Romantic drama. He used serialization and mass publication to reach working-class readers, making him one of the first truly popular literary giants. He wrote with moral urgency about injustice—capital punishment, poverty, slavery, women's rights—themes that resonated globally and continue to resonate today.
